extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, and readers interested in publication ethics and scientific publishing
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts the criteria and principles a journal used (and that commentators referred to) when deciding whether to publish, issue an Expression of Concern, or retract a controversial mathematical paper; includes procedural steps like post-publication review, author response, and invitations for rebuttal/replication. Focus is on editorial decision-making and publication-ethics handling of disputed research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors weigh reviewers' recommendations but retain final decision
rubrics_metrics.description: While reviewers make recommendations, editors make the final decision on what is acceptable for publication; editors possess the ultimate veto.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The journal noted a divergence of opinion from initial reviewers and the author mounted a scholarly response; editors face the challenge: do the concerns outweigh potential positives? They may choose publication despite reviewer concerns to encourage debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish to encourage debate / add value by stimulating open debate
rubrics_metrics.description: Does publishing a controversial approach add value to the literature through stimulating open debate? The decision to publish may be made to encourage debate, which is central to scientific research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors may accept controversial work if they judge that the debate and follow-up it provokes are beneficial. This functions as an explicit positive factor when balancing concerns about technical accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controversial papers may be published because science is a work in progress
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that a controversial paper may eventually be shown to contain flaws; science moves forward through challenges to existing paradigms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors may allow publication of paradigm-challenging work on the view that fostering debate and experimentation outweighs immediate technical concerns. The history of science includes many non-linear advances; a journal need not only publish mainstream-confirming papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal remit includes publishing work difficult to place elsewhere and using open peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: The journal has a remit to publish research appropriate for publication and which may be difficult to publish in more traditional journals; its open peer review model allows readers to explore the review history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At the time of assessment the paper 'passed that test' in the editors' view. Open peer review is cited as part of the justification: transparency lets readers judge the review process themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent post-publication assessment and public commentary
rubrics_metrics.description: Following publication, independent assessors performed post-publication peer review and made their commentary available publicly alongside the author's responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These public commentaries let readers see dissenting analyses; the journal used their existence and the lack of consensus among them as part of the rationale for not retracting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of consensus among assessors may argue against retraction
rubrics_metrics.description: As the reader may note, there is no consensus on this work, which is why the journal has opted not to retract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retraction decisions may be withheld when independent assessments do not reach agreement; the journal used absence of consensus as a reason to issue/maintain an Expression of Concern rather than retract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressions of Concern (EoC) are provisional and not the final word
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressions of concern are, by definition, not intended to be the final word on a paper; they serve as an interim notice while investigation or post-publication review continues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The journal published a provisional EoC when post-publication peer-review began and later issued an updated EoC summarizing their investigation and conclusions. The piece criticizes that an 'updated EoC' can seem odd, but acknowledges the EoC's provisional role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trigger post-publication (post hoc) assessment when technical accuracy is questioned
rubrics_metrics.description: Following peer review and publication, correspondence expressing concern about the technical accuracy of a paper can prompt an independent post hoc assessment of the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should investigate substantive technical complaints raised by readers (private emails or public comments) and may publish the results of those investigations or public commentary alongside the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invite and welcome replication studies and rebuttals
rubrics_metrics.description: The journal permits and actively encourages replication studies and invites readers to submit either a replication or rebuttal of the author's work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors explicitly encourage interested readers to submit replication or rebuttal work to 'openly articulate and formalize the technical issues.' This is cited as an alternative to retraction or as a way to resolve disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer correspondents the opportunity to publish formal rebuttals
rubrics_metrics.description: Correspondents critiquing the decision to publish the paper were offered the opportunity to publish a rebuttal; to date they have declined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The journal encourages critics to make open contributions (rebuttals) rather than only publicly criticizing editorial decisions; failing to submit formal rebuttals is treated as a factor in the editorial stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain confidentiality and engage the author during investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors sought the author's response confidentially (without revealing names of the complainers), published a provisional EoC when post-publication review began, and kept the author informed and invited responses to post-publication peer reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The process described emphasizes confidentiality of complainants and procedural fairness by involving the author and sharing opportunities to respond before final editorial conclusions are reached.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discipline-specific nature of dispute: in mathematics, demonstrable errors are not 'controversy'
rubrics_metrics.description: Commentators argued that the problem with the paper is a mathematical error that is inescapable (e.g., claiming a construction impossible by Hurwitz's theorem), so this is not merely a divergence of opinion but a demonstrable error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For mathematics, where correctness of proofs and constructions is (in principle) decidable, editors and journals should treat clear, irrefutable mathematical errors as errors rather than framing them as open controversies to be 'taught.' The anti-pattern is treating objective mathematical mistakes as legitimate 'controversies.'
